also: open the window to let air in

terms.gloss: blow through; in the passive, of a room or building, be aired
terms.grammar: the wind is the subject; of the room, the passive: cubiculum perflātur
evidence: Varr. RR 1.13: fenestrās habēre oportet ex eā partī, unde commodissimē perflārī possit
Varr. RR 1.57: in grānāria sublīmia, quae perflentur ventō
Cic. Rep. 2.11: collēs enim sunt, quī cum perflantur ipsī tum adferunt umbram vallibus
terms.comment: Latin says it from the wind’s side: a room is aired when the wind blows through it, perflātur, and a person airs it by opening the windows so that it may be: fenestrās aperīre, ut cubiculum perflētur. That sentence is ours, made of classical words; Varro uses the verb of barns and granaries and Cicero of hills open to the wind. For the air itself, see “air”.

phrases.english: Let’s open the windows and air the room.

phrases.latin: Hīc gravis est āēr; aperī paulisper fenestram.
phrases.english: It’s stuffy in here; open the window for a bit.

phrases.latin: Fenestrās habēre oportet ex eā partī, unde commodissimē perflārī possit.
phrases.english: It should have its windows on the side from which the wind can blow through it most easily.
